segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “To the angel of the assembly in Ephesus write: ‘Thus says the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works, your labor and your endurance, and that you cannot bear evil people. You have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you have found them false.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You have endurance, and you have borne up for the sake of my name, and you have not grown weary.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have this against you: you have left the love you had at first.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Remember, then, from where you have fallen; turn back and do the works you did at first. If not, I am coming to you, and I will remove your lampstand from its place—unless you turn back.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But this you do have: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Smyrna write: ‘Thus says the First and the Last, who was dead and came to life:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your affliction and your poverty—yet you are rich—and the slander from those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not be afraid of anything you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison so that you may be tested, and you will have affliction for ten days. Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies. The one who conquers will certainly not be harmed by the second death.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Pergamum write: ‘Thus says the one who has the sharp two-edged sword:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know where you live—where Satan’s throne is. Yet you hold fast to my name, and you did not deny your faith in me even in the days of Antipas, my witness, my faithful one, who was killed among you, where Satan lives.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have a few things against you: you have there some who hold fast to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel—to eat food sacrificed to idols and to commit sexual immorality.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So you too have some who in the same way hold fast to the teaching of the Nicolaitans.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So turn back. If not, I am coming to you soon, and I will make war against them with the sword of my mouth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies. To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And to the angel of the assembly in Thyatira write: ‘Thus says the Son of God, whose eyes are like a flame of fire and whose feet are like burnished bronze:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know your works—your love and faith and service and endurance—and that your last works are greater than the first.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I have this against you: you tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, and she teaches and misleads my slaves to commit sexual immorality and to eat food sacrificed to idols.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I gave her time to turn back, but she is not willing to turn back from her sexual immorality.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, I am throwing her onto a sickbed, and those who commit adultery with her into great affliction, unless they turn back from her works,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and I will kill her children with pestilence. And all the assemblies will know that I am the one who searches minds and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But to the rest of you in Thyatira, all who do not hold this teaching, who have not come to know the deep things of Satan, as they call them, I say: I am laying no other burden on you;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: only hold fast to what you have until I come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end—to that one I will give authority over the nations,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and that one will shepherd them with an iron rod, as clay pots are smashed to pieces,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: just as I myself have received authority from my Father. And I will give that one the morning star.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has an ear hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies.’

notes.note: The traditional rendering is ‘church’, which nearly all translations keep and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas ‘church’ now suggests a building or an institution. ‘Assembly’ is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

The Greek word means ‘messenger’ and can refer to a human envoy as well as a heavenly being. Everywhere else in Revelation it means a heavenly angel, and most scholars take it so here, as a heavenly representative of each community. Others think of a human leader or courier of the assembly, since the messages address the angel as responsible for the community's conduct.

The Greek formula was already old-fashioned in the first century. Readers knew it from the Greek Scriptures as the way the prophets introduced a word from God (‘Thus says the Lord’), and it also had the ring of a royal decree. The slightly archaic English is deliberate.

Most translations keep ‘repent’ as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English, however, ‘repent’ centres on feeling sorry, while the Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. Here the command is paired with resuming former works, which fits that sense.

Nothing certain is known about this group beyond what Revelation says. Verses 14–15 associate their teaching with eating food sacrificed to idols and sexual immorality, which suggests they favoured accommodation to the surrounding pagan culture. Later Christian writers connected them with the Nicolaus of Acts 6:5, but that link may be a guess from the name.

The author, himself a Jew, is writing about a specific local conflict in Smyrna, apparently involving denunciation of the believers (‘slander’). His claim is that these particular opponents have forfeited the name ‘Jews’, which he treats as a title of honour. It is polemic within a first-century dispute over who are the true people of God, not a statement about the Jewish people. The phrase has a long history of misuse against Jews.

The Greek word normally denotes a wreath or garland, such as was awarded to victors in athletic contests or worn at festivals, not a king's jewelled diadem. A first-century reader would have pictured a victor's wreath. ‘Of life’ most likely means the wreath that consists in life itself.

Pergamum was a leading centre of Roman administration and of emperor worship in the province of Asia, and was also known for its great altar of Zeus and its shrine of the healing god Asclepius. Scholars have proposed each of these as the reference, and it remains uncertain. The imperial cult is the most commonly favoured explanation, since refusal to take part in it could be fatal, as Antipas's death suggests.

In Numbers 25 Israelite men are drawn into sexual relations with Moabite women and into the worship of their gods, and Numbers 31:16 blames this on Balaam's advice. Later Jewish tradition developed Balaam into the model of a teacher who leads God's people astray. The name is used here as a label for a teaching current in Pergamum, not as a claim that anyone invoked Balaam.

The verb covers unlawful sexual activity of any kind. In the prophets, and often in Revelation, the same language is a standing metaphor for unfaithfulness to God through idolatry. It is disputed whether literal sexual conduct, participation in pagan worship, or both are meant here and in verses 20–21. The translation keeps the literal wording and leaves the question open.

The word means a small stone or pebble. Such pebbles were used for voting, including a white one for acquittal in court, and similar tokens could serve as tickets of admission to feasts or as amulets inscribed with a name. Which custom lies behind the image is uncertain, and scholars have not reached agreement.

The Greek word occurs only here and in Revelation 1:15 and is not found in earlier Greek literature. It clearly denotes some gleaming copper alloy, but exactly which metal is unknown. ‘Burnished bronze’ is a conventional approximation.

Most translations have ‘servants’. The Greek word ordinarily meant a slave, someone owned by and wholly at the disposal of a master. In the Greek Scriptures it is also an honourable title for those who belong to God, such as Moses and the prophets. ‘Slaves’ keeps the sense of belonging that a first-century reader would have heard.

Almost certainly a symbolic name, not the woman's own. Jezebel was the queen who promoted the worship of Baal in Israel (1 Kings 16–21; 2 Kings 9). The name casts this influential prophetic teacher in Thyatira in that role. Some manuscripts read ‘your wife Jezebel’, but the shorter reading is generally preferred.

The Greek says literally ‘kill with death’. In the Greek Scriptures ‘death’ frequently stands for the Hebrew word for plague, and Revelation 6:8 uses it in that sense, so ‘pestilence’ is likely here, especially after the sickbed of verse 22. The alternative is to take the phrase as a Semitic intensive, ‘strike dead’, as a number of translations do. ‘Her children’ probably means her followers.

Literally ‘kidneys and hearts’; the kidneys were regarded as the seat of a person's innermost feelings and motives. The sentence echoes Jeremiah 17:10, where it is God who searches heart and kidneys and repays each according to their deeds. Here the risen Jesus claims that role.

The same Greek word is rendered ‘Gentiles’ elsewhere in this translation where it means the non-Jewish peoples as distinct from Israel. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so ‘nations’ is used. Verses 26–27 draw on Psalm 2:8–9.

Most translations have ‘rule’. The verb means to tend a flock and was a common image for a king's government. It comes from the Greek version of Psalm 2:9, where the Hebrew text as traditionally read has ‘break’. Given the smashed pots, some scholars think the sense here is closer to ‘devastate’. ‘Shepherd’ is kept so that the image matches the other places Revelation uses the verb (7:17; 12:5; 19:15).

A key refrain in Revelation and the Johannine writings, where translators vary between ‘conquer’, ‘overcome’ and ‘be victorious’; the repetition is lost if the English varies.

Recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation as ‘tribulation’, ‘affliction’, ‘distress’ or ‘suffering’, and ‘great tribulation’ has become a technical term that a consistent rendering should either keep or deliberately replace.
With its verb it recurs across the New Testament as ‘fornication’, ‘sexual immorality’ or ‘prostitution’, and Revelation's metaphorical use needs to stay visibly linked to the literal use elsewhere.
With its verb σκανδαλίζω it is frequent in the Gospels and Paul, and translators vary between ‘stumbling block’, ‘trap’, ‘offence’ and ‘cause to sin’.
